title: Speaking Without Notes
tagline: A Roman lawyer who could repeat a whole day's auction from memory, and a way to give a talk with a house instead of a script.
card: The five parts of ancient rhetoric, and how to turn a talk into a short walk through a palace so you can speak without reading.
goal: you will learn the five canons of rhetoric, turn a talk into five or six pictures, place them in a palace and deliver it from the walk.

left_off.q: How does a champion memorise a whole pack of cards faster than 52 pictures?
left_off.a: By taking two or three cards at a time and building one person-action-object scene for them, so a pack needs about 17 scenes.

left_off.q: In our card system, what is the Ace of Spades, and what is the King of Clubs?
Why must the picture for a card always be the same?
left_off.a: So the system is automatic and you never have to decide again.

text: Rome, about a hundred years before the birth of Christ. Quintus Hortensius Hortalus, a famous lawyer, was known for a memory that his friends found hard to believe. He could listen to a long argument in court, and then stand up and answer every point in turn, without a note.

According to the writer Seneca the Elder, who tells the story a century later, his friends once made a bet. Hortensius sat through a whole day at an auction, listening to the sales. In the evening he stood up and recited, in order, everything that had been sold, who bought it and for how much. The auctioneer's clerk checked the records. Hortensius did not make a single mistake.

check.q: What did Hortensius do after the auction?
check.a: He recited everything that had been sold, with the buyers and prices, in order, and the records agreed.

parts.talk: Is it more impressive to remember a day of speeches or a day of prices? Which would you find harder?

text: To Hortensius and the men he competed with, this was not a party trick. A Roman orator had to speak for hours in public with no screen, no cards, and no microphone. The ancient teachers of public speaking, whose books we still have, divided their art into five parts, and memory was one of them.

The five were: finding what to say, putting it in order, choosing the words, keeping it in mind, and delivering it with voice and gesture. A speaker who forgot his place lost the case. So memory was taught as carefully as grammar.

check.q: Why did Roman orators need memory so much?
check.a: They spoke for hours with no notes, screens or microphones, and losing the thread could lose the case.

parts.talk: What is the longest you have spoken in public without notes? How did you feel?

text: Today we give talks with slides, and most of us still read from them, which is why so many talks are dull. A speaker who reads loses the audience. A speaker who looks up, who has the talk in their head and the audience in their eyes, is a different person.

This is exactly what the palace method makes possible. You do not memorise a script word for word. You memorise five or six pictures in five or six places, and the words come as you walk. The Romans did it that way, and you can too.

check.q: What do you memorise for a talk, if not the script?
check.a: A few strong pictures, one for each main point, placed in a route you can walk.

parts.talk: Think of a talk you have to give soon. What is its main point in one sentence?

words.m: a main rule or part of an art. The five canons of rhetoric.
the art of speaking or writing in a way that persuades.
a person who is skilled at public speaking.
a sale where things go to the person who offers the most money.
the way you speak: voice, pace and gesture.
the move from one part of a talk to the next.

source: Hortensius's feat is reported by Seneca the Elder, Controversiae, preface to Book 1. The five parts of rhetoric are set out in Cicero and the Rhetorica ad Herennium. Told here in our own words.
method_heading: A talk in five or six rooms

method.x: The ancient teachers named five parts of rhetoric. The fourth one, memory, is the part you are learning here, and the other four tell you what to put in your palace.

items.h: Write the talk as five or six points.
items.x: An opening hook, three main points and a closing. One line each.

items.h: Turn each point into one vivid picture.
items.x: Not the words: the idea. A sad moon for 'sleep problems'.

items.h: Choose a palace with the same number of places.
items.x: A short route you know well: door, hall, kitchen, stairs, bedroom.

items.h: Place the pictures along the route.
items.x: In the order of the talk. The walk is the structure.
Say the talk aloud as you move through the palace, ten minutes at a time.

items.h: Add a calming ritual for the moment before you speak.
items.x: A slow breath, a hand on the table, and a picture of the first place.

method.title: A talk on why sleep matters
method.given: Five points: hook, three reasons, call to action.
lines: A giant yawning moon is sitting on the doorstep, with a pillow for a face: 'Who slept badly last night?'
A filing cabinet in the hall, with sleeping drawers snoring as each memory is put in.
A grumpy toast is leaping from the toaster, shouting at the butter.
A bandaged heart is climbing the stairs, panting.
A bed with a clock saying 10 p.m. and a big green tick.
method.pic: As you walk in, a yawning moon on the doorstep starts the talk, and the rest follows as you go from room to room.

method.x: Four tips from the old teachers

items: Remember ideas, not sentences. The words will come, and fresh words sound alive.
Keep a spare place for the moment your mind goes blank: a picture that says 'start the next point'.
Rehearse out loud. Practise the sound of speaking, not only the thought.
Practise on a walk. Moving helps your mind link the words to places.

method.x: Give a one-minute talk aloud about a subject you know, walking through the five rooms of the sleep example or your own.

try.title: The five canons
try.prompt: Match each canon to its meaning.

try.title: Plan a short talk
try.prompt: Choose a topic you know well. Write five points (hook, three points, closing) and one vivid picture for each.
try.model: Topic: Why walk to work. 1 Hook: a pair of enormous boots stomping down the street. 2 Health: a heart wearing running shoes. 3 Money: a piggy bank growing legs. 4 Mood: a cloud that gets blown away. 5 Close: a footprint with a green tick.
checks: Each has a picture, not a sentence.
The pictures are different from each other.

try.title: Place it
try.prompt: Put your five pictures at five places of a palace you know, in order. Write where each one goes and what it is doing there.
try.model: 1 Front door: the boots stamp on the doormat. 2 Hall: the heart is jogging up and down the hall. 3 Kitchen: the piggy bank walks into the fridge. 4 Stairs: the cloud drifts down them, clearing the air. 5 Bedroom: a giant footprint is on the pillow with a green tick.
checks: Each picture is at a different place.
The places are in my usual route.

items.s: A talk for a five-point route needs ___ places.
We memorise the walk, not the ___.
The fourth canon of rhetoric is ___.

try.q: Why is it better to memorise pictures than a script?
opts: You can speak naturally and recover if you lose your place
try.why: Pictures give you the sequence and the ideas, and the words stay fresh.

try.title: Give the talk
try.prompt: Give your five-point talk aloud in two minutes, walking through the palace in your head.

cards: Roman lawyer, reported to have recited a whole auction's sales in order.

quiz.q: How many canons of rhetoric are there?
What does a speaker memorise in the palace method?
opts: A picture for each main point, placed along a route
quiz.why: A short chain of strong pictures and places.

opts: You practise the sound and pace of speaking as well as the thought
quiz.why: Delivery is the fifth canon, and it needs voice practice.

opts: A picture that tells you where to restart if your mind goes blank
quiz.why: A safety net for a blank moment.

challenge.title: Memory challenge: the five canons
challenge.intro: Learn the five canons in order, with a picture for each. A lightbulb, a row of boxes, a paintbrush, a treasure chest, a trumpet.
challenge.study: Place the five pictures in five places. Invention at the door, then onwards.

look_back.q: In the card system, what suit stands for Asia?
What do you do with the name after you hear it?
look_back.a: Say it at once and use it in the conversation.

look_back.q: When is a story chain better than a palace?
look_back.a: For a short list you need quickly and have no place for.

look_back.q: What is the method of loci?
look_back.a: Placing pictures at places along a fixed route.

turn a talk into five pictures and place them.
